blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Fools You
blocks.text: Cut a pineapple open and it looks like one fruit, but it is really made of dozens of small fruits fused together. Each rough bump on the skin, called an eye, started as its own flower. The plant grows a spike of flowers, and as they swell they merge into a single sweet fruit. That is why one pineapple can have a hundred eyes. The pineapple plant surprises people too. It is not a tree. It is a low, spiky plant, and it is related to the mosses that hang from trees in warm places. Each plant grows only one pineapple at a time, and that takes about two years. Pineapples come from South America. Long ago, sailors carried them across the ocean to Europe, where the fruit was so rare that only rich people could taste it. Some people even rented a pineapple just to show it off at a party, then gave it back.

blocks.prompt: A Fruit Fit for a King
blocks.text: A pineapple is one of the strangest fruits you can buy. What looks like a single fruit is actually many fruits grown together. Each diamond shape on the skin, called an eye, began as a separate flower. As the flowers ripen they fuse into one solid, sweet mass around a woody core. Count the spirals of eyes and you find a hidden pattern: they usually curve in two directions, often eight one way and thirteen the other, the same number sequence that shows up in pinecones and sunflowers. The plant itself is humble. It is not a tree but a low bush of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, and it grows only one pineapple every year or two. Farmers can snap the leafy crown off the top, push it into soil, and grow a brand new plant from it. Fresh pineapple carries a chemical called bromelain. Bromelain breaks down protein, which is why eating a lot of raw pineapple can make your tongue feel tingly or sore. Cooks use the same power to soften tough meat before cooking. When European sailors first brought pineapples home from South America, the fruit became a symbol of wealth. They were so hard to grow in cold countries that a single pineapple could cost as much as a small house, and hosts displayed one at a feast to show off.

blocks.prompt: The Pineapple's Long Journey
blocks.text: To a botanist, a pineapple is not really a fruit at all. It is a whole cluster of fruits, dozens of them, fused into one body. Each scaly section on the surface, called an eye, is the ripened remains of a single flower. The plant sends up a spike crowded with flowers, and as they mature they swell and knit together around a central stalk. The tuft of stiff leaves on top is a small shoot that can be planted to grow an entirely new pineapple. The plant grows low to the ground and belongs to the bromeliad family, the same group as the gray Spanish moss that drapes southern trees. A single plant produces just one pineapple, and the wait can stretch to two years or more. The fruit came from the tropical lowlands of South America, where Indigenous people had grown it for centuries and called it by a Tupi word, nanas, meaning excellent fruit. In 1493 the crew of Christopher Columbus met the pineapple on a Caribbean island and carried it back to Europe. Because its rough skin looked like a pine cone, the Spanish named it piña, and English speakers added apple, the old word for any fruit, to make pineapple. In cold Europe the pineapple was nearly impossible to grow, so it became a badge of wealth and welcome. Wealthy families built heated glass houses just to raise a few, and a ripe pineapple at the center of a table announced that the host could afford anything. Carvings of pineapples still decorate gateposts and staircases as a sign of hospitality. Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme called bromelain that digests protein. It is the reason raw pineapple can sting the tongue, the reason it tenderizes meat, and the reason it refuses to let gelatin set into jelly. Heat destroys the enzyme, so canned pineapple behaves quite differently from fresh. One warning worth knowing: a pineapple does not grow sweeter after it is picked. Unlike a banana, it must be harvested ripe, which is why shipping the fresh fruit long distances has always been a challenge.

blocks.prompt: Forever a King's Fruit: How the Pineapple Fooled Everyone
blocks.text: Few foods have fooled as many people as the pineapple, starting with what it even is. Slice one open and it seems like a single fruit, but a botanist sees a crowd. A pineapple is a multiple fruit, a fusion of dozens of separate berries that each grew from its own flower and then swelled together into one body. Every rough, diamond-shaped eye on the skin marks where one of those flowers once sat. If you count the spirals those eyes form, you find them curving in two directions at once, commonly eight rows spiraling one way and thirteen the other. Those are Fibonacci numbers, the same efficient packing pattern that governs pinecones, sunflower heads, and the scales of many seed cones. The plant is just as surprising. It is no tree. It is a squat rosette of tough, spiny leaves belonging to the bromeliad family, a relative of the Spanish moss that hangs from oaks in the American South. A single plant labors for roughly two years to produce exactly one pineapple, and the leafy crown twisted off the top can be rooted to start the cycle again. The fruit began in the lowlands of South America, where Indigenous peoples cultivated it long before Europeans arrived and named it nanas, an excellent fruit, in the Tupi language. In 1493, sailors with Christopher Columbus encountered it on the Caribbean island of Guadeloupe. To Spanish eyes the spiky fruit resembled a pinecone, so they called it piña; English later fastened on apple, the old catchall word for fruit, producing pineapple. In the cold cities of Europe the pineapple became something close to treasure. Growing one demanded a heated glass hothouse, called a pinery, and years of a gardener's patience, so a ripe pineapple could cost a small fortune. Guests who could not afford to eat one would rent a pineapple for a single evening to crown their table, then return it. The fruit became shorthand for wealth and welcome, which is why carved pineapples still perch on gateposts, bedposts, and staircases as a sign of hospitality. Two facts keep the pineapple interesting on the plate. First, its flesh is loaded with bromelain, an enzyme that dismantles protein. Bromelain is why raw pineapple can leave your tongue raw, why it tenderizes tough meat, and why fresh pineapple will not let gelatin set: the enzyme chews up the very protein that would form the jelly. Cooking or canning destroys bromelain, which is why canned pineapple sets in a dessert while fresh pineapple ruins it. Second, a pineapple does not sweeten after harvest the way a banana does, because it stores little starch to convert into sugar. It must be picked ripe, a stubborn fact that once made the fresh fruit almost impossible to ship until refrigerated transport and Hawaiian plantations, driven by companies like Dole, finally put pineapple within everyone's reach in the twentieth century.
